I have worked in multiple labs and collaborated with researchers from diverse disciplines: engineering, computer science, genomics, virology, and clinical medicine. What connects all of it is one idea about the human body.

## The body as an engineered system

I see the human body as the most complex engineered system we know, and I study it the way an engineer studies any system: layer by layer.

At the top is the whole system, the body. It is built from organs, organs from tissues, and tissues from cells. Inside each cell, the nucleus holds the chromosomes, and the chromosomes hold DNA, the source code. That code is transcribed into RNA, RNA is translated into proteins, and proteins carry out the functions that keep everything running.

If DNA is the code, the rest of the body is the hardware it runs on. Organs act as actuators. Physiological signals like heart rate, temperature, and hydration are the system's telemetry, readable with the right sensors. Underneath, the cellular machinery runs thousands of processes in parallel, like an operating system running many threads at once. Complex, but traceable.

I believe this system can be fundamentally studied and understood through hardware–software co-design: sensors and devices that measure the body, paired with computational and AI methods that make sense of what they measure. Everything below is that idea applied at a different layer.

## Learning from scarce, noisy data

Biomedical AI has a problem most AI doesn't: there is rarely enough data, and what exists is noisy. My Ph.D. took that on directly. The same diffusion models that turn random noise into realistic images can turn it into realistic biomedical data. My hypothesis is that by combining domain knowledge (physics constraints), hardware–AI co-design, and generative models, we can create synthetic biomedical data that makes both sensing and modeling more reliable. This became my dissertation, *Generative and Domain-Informed Modeling of Biomedical Signals Under Data Scarcity and Real-World Noise* (UMass Lowell, 2026).

## Hydration: the underrated vital sign

The other half of my Ph.D. continued my Master's work: a [non-invasive optical wearable that tracks hydration](projects/wearable-hydration/index.qmd). I believe hydration is one of the most important and most undervalued health metrics we have. It shapes cognition, physical performance, and recovery, yet unlike heart rate or sleep, almost nobody measures it continuously. I led the project end to end, from the IRB protocol and data collection to machine-learning models running on the device, validated against saliva measurements.

## Multi-omics: reading every layer of the code

Most of my work today sits at the bottom of the stack, in the source code itself. Each omics technology reads a different layer of the same system. The genome (DNA) is the code. Chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) shows which parts of that code are open and readable in a given cell. The transcriptome (RNA-seq) shows which parts are actually running. Proteins and metabolites are the output. No single layer explains a disease; integrating them, often one cell at a time, is how you start to see the system instead of a single component.

The goal is to turn that understanding into outcomes: better understanding and treatment of infectious disease, earlier cancer detection, and personalized health monitoring.

## Still an engineer at heart

My background is in electronics design, and I still use it: I have developed wearables by integrating sensors, firmware, and on-device AI into working prototypes. On the computational side, I build reproducible Nextflow pipelines, like my open-source [RNA splicing pipeline](https://github.com/NazimBL/splicing-analysis-pipeline), and GPU-accelerated workflows on HPC. I also build platforms that give biologists AI-powered analysis without writing code, like [MotifXplorer](projects/motif-xplorer/index.qmd), co-developed with the Takaku lab at the University of North Dakota.

You can explore these projects in more detail on my [Projects Page](projects.qmd).
